extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning discrete mathematics and proof techniques (mathematical induction, relations, countability)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for constructing proofs and objects in discrete math: building the transitive closure of a relation by recursion/induction, working with relation powers and paths, and methods for proving sets are countable or denumerable. Includes theorem statements, constructive definitions, and proof strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of transitive closure
rubrics_metrics.description: The transitive closure of R is the smallest relation S on A such that R ⊆ S and S is transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State explicitly the three goals when proving a set is the transitive closure: (1) R ⊆ S, (2) S is transitive, and (3) for every T, if R ⊆ T ⊆ A×A and T is transitive, then S ⊆ T. Use a named S for clarity and handle each goal in turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing transitive closure via relation powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Define R1 = R and for every n ≥ 1, R_{n+1} = R_n ◦ R, then the transitive closure S is ∪_{n∈Z+} R_n (Theorem 6.5.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation: if (a0,a1),(a1,a2),...,(a_{n-1},a_n) ∈ R then (a0,a_n) ∈ R^n. Use recursion to define the R^n and prove properties by induction. To show S is the smallest transitive superset, prove R^n ⊆ any transitive superset T by induction on n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive definition of R^n
rubrics_metrics.description: R1 = R; for every n ≥ 1, R_{n+1} = R_n ◦ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recursive definition formalizes the ellipsis-argument from examples: compositions of R correspond to paths of increasing lengths. Use recursion to facilitate inductive proofs about R^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: R_{m+n} = R_m ◦ R_n
rubrics_metrics.description: For all positive integers m and n, R_{m+n} = R_m ◦ R_n (Lemma 6.5.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by fixing one index (e.g., m) and doing induction on the other (n). Base case n=1 uses definition; induction step uses associativity of composition and the recursive definition R_{n+1}=R_n ◦ R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving transitivity of S = ∪ R^n
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove S is transitive, let (x,y) ∈ S and (y,z) ∈ S; choose n,m with (x,y) ∈ R^n and (y,z) ∈ R^m and use Lemma R_{m+n}=R_m ◦ R_n to get (x,z) ∈ R^{m+n} ⊆ S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce witness integers n and m for existential membership statements. The key is constructing a witness (k = m + n) to satisfy the existential goal (x,z) ∈ R^k. This is a standard pattern for existential conclusions in inductive/recursive settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving minimality of S (smallest transitive superset)
rubrics_metrics.description: If R ⊆ T ⊆ A×A and T is transitive, then show S ⊆ T by proving ∀n ∈ Z+ (R^n ⊆ T) via induction on n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base: R^1 = R ⊆ T by assumption. Induction step: assume R^n ⊆ T; take arbitrary (x,y) ∈ R^{n+1}, use recursive definition to find z with (x,z) ∈ R and (z,y) ∈ R^n, then apply R ⊆ T, inductive hypothesis, and transitivity of T to conclude (x,y) ∈ T. This exemplifies the standard technique: to prove set inclusion show an arbitrary element belongs to the target set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-writing strategy: naming sets & breaking goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Naming frequently-used sets at the start (e.g., S = ∪ R^n) and decomposing the definition-based goals into separate claims helps structure proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary emphasizes: (i) define S early, (ii) prove R⊆S, S transitive, and minimality one at a time, and (iii) when a proof step is omitted in text, work out details yourself. This is an explicit rubric for clarity and completeness in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using induction to prove algebraic formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Example (Theorem 6.5.3): For fixed b, prove by induction on a that (2^b − 1)·(Σ_{k=0}^{a-1} 2^{kb}) = 2^{ab} − 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose which variable to induct on (fix other variables), establish base case explicitly, and in the induction step manipulate algebraic expressions using the induction hypothesis to reach the desired form. Show the algebraic rearrangements clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure of a set under a function via intersection of closed supersets
rubrics_metrics.description: Let F = {C | B ⊆ C ⊆ A and C is closed under f}. Prove F ≠ ∅ and that ⋂F is the closure of B under f (exercise 1(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a standard method: show the family of closed supersets is nonempty (at least A ∈ F), then the intersection of all such supersets is the smallest closed set containing B. Make the minimality argument explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure of a set under a function via iterates (union of images)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define B1 = B; for every n ≥ 1 define B_{n+1} = f(B_n) = {f(x) | x ∈ B_n}. Then ⋃_{n∈Z+} B_n is the closure of B under f (exercise 1(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constructive approach parallels the construction of transitive closure. Use recursion/induction to prove the union is closed and minimal. This method often yields a concrete description of the closure in terms of reachable elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure under a family of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a family F of functions from A to A and B ⊆ A, the closure of B under F exists (exercise 3), i.e., the smallest C with B ⊆ C ⊆ A and C closed under every f ∈ F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either intersect all closed supersets or iterate under the whole family (analogous to single-function iteration). The same minimality arguments apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure under binary operations (A×A→A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A×A → A and B ⊆ A, define closure of B under f as smallest C with B ⊆ C ⊆ A and ∀x,y ∈ C, f(x,y) ∈ C; prove existence by intersection or iterative construction (exercise 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret closure requirements carefully for n-ary operations; recursive construction uses images under f of pairs drawn from previous stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity of relation powers
rubrics_metrics.description: If R ⊆ S are relations on A, then for every positive integer n, R^n ⊆ S^n (exercise 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by induction on n using the recursive definition R^{n+1}=R^n ◦ R and the monotonicity of composition: if X⊆Y and U⊆V then X◦U ⊆ Y◦V (argue elementwise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation powers ↔ path interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: For all n ∈ Z+, R^n = {(a,b) ∈ A×A | there is an R-path from a to b of length n}. Moreover, if S is the transitive closure, S = {(a,b) ∈ A×A | there is an R-path from a to b} (exercise 10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use induction on n to show equivalence between composition definition and existence of paths. This provides an intuitive graph/path perspective on relation powers and closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance in the transitive closure
rubrics_metrics.description: If S is transitive closure of R and (a,b) ∈ S, define d(a,b) as the smallest positive integer n with (a,b) ∈ R^n (exercise 9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the well-ordering principle to ensure existence of smallest n. Prove properties like d(a,c) ≤ d(a,b) + d(b,c) (triangle inequality) and decomposition: if d(a,c)=N and 0<m<N then there exists b with d(a,b)=m and d(b,c)=N−m.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple R-paths and characterization of S minus diagonal
rubrics_metrics.description:
A simple R-path is an R-path f : J_n → A that is one-to-one. For all n, R^n 
eq A ⊆ {(a,b) | there is a simple R-path from a to b of length ≤ n}, and S 
eq A = {(a,b) | there is a simple R-path from a to b} (exercise 11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use injectivity of the path to bound lengths and characterize pairs connected by simple paths. This is useful for arguments truncating the union of powers when A is finite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bound for transitive closure on finite sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If A has m elements and S is transitive closure of R, then S = R ∪ R^2 ∪ ... ∪ R^m = ⋃_{1≤n≤m} R^n (exercise 13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the maximum possible length of a simple R-path (≤ m) to show no new pairs appear beyond R^m; rely on previous exercises about simple paths and distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of equinumerous and finite sets (cardinality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A ∼ B iff there is a one-to-one, onto function f : A → B. For each natural n let I_n = {i ∈ Z+ | i ≤ n}. A is finite if there exists n with I_n ∼ A; otherwise A is infinite. The number of elements |A| is the unique n with I_n ∼ A (Definition 7.1.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Countability is framed via bijections; proving finiteness/count involves constructing explicit bijections or showing existence/uniqueness of such n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to prove sets equinumerous (explicit bijections)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show A ∼ B give an explicit one-to-one, onto function f : A → B and verify injectivity and surjectivity (examples: Z+ ∼ Z via f defined piecewise; Z+×Z+ ∼ Z+ via formula f(i,j) = (i+j−2)(i+j−1)/2 + i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common technique: provide an explicit formula, then check injectivity by case analysis and surjectivity by construction of preimages for an arbitrary target element. Tables/diagrams can illustrate pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 7.1.2: product and disjoint union preserve equinumerosity
rubrics_metrics.description: If A ∼ B and C ∼ D then (1) A×C ∼ B×D via h(a,c)=(f(a),g(c)); (2) if A,C disjoint and B,D disjoint then A∪C ∼ B∪D (exercise 13 completes proof that f∪g is bijection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct product bijection from component bijections and handle union bijection by combining functions on disjoint domains. Prove one-to-one and onto by elementwise arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation properties of ∼ and manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation ∼ is reflexive (identity), symmetric (inverse of bijection), and transitive (composition of bijections) (Theorem 7.1.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit constructions: identity map for reflexivity, inverse map for symmetry (Theorem 5.3.4/5.3.3 referenced), composition for transitivity (Theorem 5.2.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: denumerable, countable, uncountable
rubrics_metrics.description: A is denumerable if Z+ ∼ A; A is countable if it is finite or denumerable; otherwise uncountable (Definition 7.1.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these definitions along with Theorem 7.1.5 equivalences to prove countability: either produce onto f:Z+→A or injective f:A→Z+.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalences for countability (Theorem 7.1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For set A, equivalent statements: (1) A is countable; (2) either A=∅ or there is an onto f : Z+ → A; (3) there is a one-to-one f : A → Z+.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof directions use: if A finite take filler element to extend onto map; invert onto map via well-ordering to get injection; to prove denumerability of infinite subset of Z+ list elements in increasing order and define a bijection Z+→B by recursion (exercise 14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving Q is denumerable (Theorem 7.1.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Map f : Z×Z+ → Q by f(p,q)=p/q (onto but not injective). Use known bijections Z+×Z+ ∼ Z+ and Z+ ∼ Z to obtain a one-to-one, onto map Z+→Q (compose appropriately) and apply Theorem 7.1.5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy: reduce to a denumerable domain via equinumerosity theorems, compose maps to obtain an onto map from Z+ to Q; then deduce countability/denumerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countability-preserving constructions (products, unions, countable unions, sequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorems 7.2.1, 7.2.2, 7.2.4: (1) product of countable sets is countable; (2) union of countably many countable sets is countable; (3) set of all finite sequences from a countable set is countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: map elements to Z+×Z+ then compose with bijection Z+×Z+→Z+; index families and list elements by (i,j) and use bijection Z+→Z+×Z+; for finite sequences induct on length and use append map F : S_n × A → S_{n+1} shown to be bijection to transfer countability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof approach for countable unions (Theorem 7.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the countable family F = {A_1,A_2,...} and each A_i = {a_i1,a_i2,...}. Then define f(i,j)=a_{i,j} and compose with a bijection g:Z+→Z+×Z+ to get onto map Z+→⋃F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure nonempty handling (exclude ∅ from family or treat separately). This is the standard diagonal/array listing method to enumerate countable union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countability of finite sequences (Theorem 7.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a countable set A, let S_n be sequences of length n. Prove by induction that each S_n is countable and then ⋃_{n∈N} S_n is countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base S_0={∅}. Induction: construct F : S_n × A → S_{n+1} by F(f,a)=f ∪ {(n+1,a)} and show F is bijection (exercise). Then use previous theorems that product and countable unions preserve countability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's theorem strategy (P(Z+) uncountable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show there is no onto f : Z+ → P(Z+) (Theorem 7.2.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses diagonalization idea: assume f exists and build a subset of Z+ that leads to contradiction (sketch given: 'the proof is based on statement 2 of Theorem 7.1.5'). The rubric: to show uncountability construct a set that cannot appear in the range of any purported enumeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: General inductive-proof patterns and advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Common patterns: fix one variable and induct on the other; when proving ∀ statements use arbitrary element and show property; existential goals require explicit witness construction (often from inductive hypothesis); use well-ordering principle to extract minimal elements when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text commentary repeatedly stresses these patterns (introducing variables n,m; finding witness k=m+n; proving inclusion by taking arbitrary element). Follow these templates when writing rigorous proofs by induction or recursion.
